Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.57 9.2 The orbit counting theorem Here is a question: suppose you have lots of cubes, and you want to colour their faces using three colours. How many different cubes are possible? The difficulty in the question is that you might think you’ve coloured the cubes differently, but then when you pick them up and rotate them, some will be the same. To answer this question, we need to know about the orbits of the group of rotations of a cube. We need a way of counting them. The following result is sometimes called Burnside’s Lemma, but it’s also sometimes called Not Burnside’s Lemma. In fact, it is due to Cauchy and Frobenius. Burnside just wrote about it in his book. Definition 9.2.1. Suppose Y is a G-set with action λ, and g ∈ G. Then FixY(g) = {y ∈ Y ∶ λ(g)y = y} is the set of points in Y that are fixed by g. Don’t confuse FixY(g) and StabG(y). The first is all things in Y that are fixed by g; the second is all things in G that fix y. Example 9.2.2. We know that S5 acts on Y = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. If τ = (1 2 5) and ρ = (1 2 3 4 5) are permutations in S5, then FixY(τ ) = {3, 4} and FixY(ρ) = ∅ and FixY(e) = Y. Theorem 9.2.3. (Orbit Counting Theorem.) Let G be a finite group acting on a set Y . Then: No. of orbits of G on Y = 1 ∣G∣ ∑ g∈G ∣FixY(g)∣ In other words, the number of orbits is equal to the average number of fixed points. Proof. Let P ⊆ Y × G be the set P = {(y, g) ∶ λ(g)y = y}. We count ∣P∣ in two different ways. Firstly, note that we can write P as {(y, g) ∶ g ∈ G, y ∈ FixY(g)}, and so ∣P∣ = ∑ g∈G ∣FixY(g)∣. (1) Secondly, note that we can write P as {(y, g) ∶ y ∈ Y, g ∈ StabG(y)} and so (by the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem), ∣P∣ = ∑ y∈Y ∣StabG(y)∣ = ∑ y∈Y ∣G∣ ∣Gy∣ . Now Y can be broken down as a union of disjoint orbits, Y = Orb1 ∪ . . . ∪ Orbm and for any two y, y′ ∈ Orbi we have Gy = Gy′ = Orbi. We can therefore rewrite our sum as, ∣P∣ = ∑ y∈Y ∣G∣ ∣Gy∣ = m ∑ i=1 ( ∑ y∈Orbi ∣G∣ ∣Gy∣ ) = m ∑ i=1 (∣Orbi∣ ⋅ ( ∣G∣ ∣Orbi∣ )) = m∣G∣. (2) Combining equations 1 and 2 we get, m∣G∣ = ∑ g∈G ∣FixY(g)∣. Since m is the number of orbits of G on Y , the theorem follows immediately. Example 9.2.4. Consider the group G = {e, (1 2), (3 4), (1 2)(3 4)}. It has an obvious action on the set Y = {1, 2, 3, 4} given by λ(g)y = gy for all g ∈ G and all y ∈ Y . Let’s calculate the number of orbits of G on Y using the Orbit Counting Theorem. FixY(e) = Y, FixY((1 2)) = {3, 4}, FixY((3 4)) = {1, 2}, FixY((1 2)(3 4)) = ∅. Hence the number of orbits of G on Y is m = 1 4 (4 + 2 + 2 + 0) = 2. What are these orbits? By inspection we see the two orbits are {1, 2} and {3, 4}. This example is trivial. Our next example is something harder, that will help us with the cube question.

# Page 2^page=2
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.58 9.3 An example: colouring octagons Our next example will help us with the cube question. Example 9.3.1. Suppose we colour the edges a regular octagon using three colours. How many different coloured octagons can we obtain? In the diagram below we have three such octagons, A, B, C. Notice that A and B are the same (one is just the other rotated) while C is different (it has more blue edges). Problems like this occur frequently in things like the development of pharmaceuticals. A B C Colouring the edges of three octagons using three colours Two coloured octagons are indistinguishable from each other if and only if we can move from one to the other using a symmetry of an octagon — that is if D16 can transform one coloured octagon into the other. Time to use group actions in a fancy way! Let O be an octagon whose edges are coloured using colours {r, b, g}. Let X be the set of all possible ways of edge-colouring O (starting from the top going anticlockwise), so for example A above gives us (r, r, g, b, r, g, r, b) ∈ X and B gives us (r, b, r, r, g, b, r, g) ∈ X and C gives us (b, r, g, b, r, g, r, b) ∈ X. Clearly ∣X∣ = 3 8. Now D16 acts on X in the obvious way. For example (see digram below), the usual anticlockwise rotation ρ = (1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8) ∈ D16 acts on X by sending (r, r, g, b, r, g, r, b) to (b, r, r, g, b, r, g, r). ρ Now we see that two coloured octagons are the same if and only if they lie in the same orbit of this action of D16 on X. Therefore the number of distinct ways of edge colouring an octagon using three colours is equal to the number of orbits of D16 on X. We calculate this using the Orbit Counting Lemma. For this we calculate ∣FixX(g)∣ for each g ∈ D16. Of course we have, FixX(e) = X so ∣FixX(e)∣ = 38. Now, ρ only fixes elements of X that lie in {(a, a, a, a, a, a, a, a) ∶ a ∈ {r, b, g}}, so, ∣FixX(ρ)∣ = 3.

# Page 3^page=3
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.59 On the other hand, ρ2 fixes elements of X that lie in {(a, c, a, c, a, c, a, c) ∶ a, c ∈ {r, b, g}}, so ∣FixX(ρ 2)∣ = 3 2. Continuing in this way you can work out that, ∣FixX(ρ 3)∣ = 3, ∣FixX(ρ4)∣ = 3 4, ∣FixX(ρ 5)∣ = 3, ∣FixX(ρ 6)∣ = 3 2, ∣FixX(ρ7)∣ = 3 Now let’s turn to the reflections. We can name the reflections any way we want, so let’s take σ1, σ2, σ3, σ4 to be the four reflections whose lines of reflection are through two corners, and let σ5, σ6, σ7, σ8 be the four reflections whose lines of reflection are through two edges. Two different types of reflection of O: corner-corner or edge-edge One of these reflections (through two corners) is σ1 = (2 8)(3 7)(4 6). It fixes elements of X that lie in {(a, c, d, e, e, d, c, a) ∶ a, c, d, e ∈ {r, b, g}}. Hence ∣FixX(σ1)∣ = 3 4. Reflections σ2, σ3, and σ4 are similar. Hence, ∣FixX(σ1)∣ = ∣FixX(σ2)∣ = ∣FixX(σ3)∣ = ∣FixX(σ4)∣ = 3 4. Another one of these reflections (through one edge) is σ5 = (1 2)(3 8)(4 7)(5 6). It fixes elements of X that lie in {(a, c, d, e, f, e, d, c) ∶ a, c, d, e, f ∈ {r, b, g}}. Hence ∣FixX(σ5)∣ = 35. Reflections σ6, σ7, and σ8 are similar. Hence, ∣FixX(σ5)∣ = ∣FixX(σ6)∣ = ∣FixX(σ7)∣ = ∣FixX(σ8)∣ = 3 5. Plugging all this into the Orbit Counting Theorem we have, m = 1 16 (3 8 + 3 + 3 2 + 3 + 3 4 + 3 + 3 2 + 3 + 4 ⋅ 34 + 4 ⋅ 3 5) = 7968 16 = 498.

# Page 4^page=4
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.60 9.4 Solving the cube question Example 9.4.1. If you colour the faces of a cube using three colours, how many different coloured cubes can you obtain? Try to work this out as an exercise, but be careful here: a cube is 3D in 3D space, whereas the octagon in Example 9.3.1 was 2D in 3D space. We could reflect the octagon (by “flipping” it through the 3rd dimension). However, we can’t do this with a cube because it is 3D — a reflected 3D object is fundamentally different from the original object (e.g. your right and left hands). After you’ve tried this exercise, an outline of the solution is given below. (Hint: make sure you only consider rotational symmetries). Outline solution. We described the full symmetry group of a cube C in Example 3.3.2. However, as mentioned above, two coloured cubes are only the same if you can get from one to the other using rotations (since reflections change the object). Therefore the group we are interested in is Rot(C). We described the group Rot(C) of rotations of a cube C in Example 3.3.2. Look back at this example, and remind yourself we have: • One identity rotation — type (A) • Six 90 degree face rotations — type (B) • Three 180 degree face rotations — type (C) • Eight 120 corner rotations — type (D) • Six 180 edge rotations — type (E) So 24 symmetries. Now (as in Example 3.3.2) we let X be the set of all possible ways of face- colouring C, and note that Rot(C) acts on X in the obvious way. We have that ∣X∣ = 3 6 because there are 3 choices for the colour on each face. Now think about the face-colourings of C that are fixed by the elements of Rot(C) (it helps here to look back at the diagrams in Example 3.3.2). • The type (A) rotation g fixes all possible face-colourings, so ∣FixX(g)∣ = 3 6. • Each type (B) rotation g fixes all face-colourings in which the top and bottom faces receive any colour and the sides all receive the same colour, so ∣FixX(g)∣ = 3 3. • Each type (C) rotation g satisfies ∣FixX(g)∣ = 3 4 • Each type (D) rotation g satisfies ∣FixX(g)∣ = 3 2 • Each type (E) rotation g satisfies ∣FixX(g)∣ = 3 3. Plugging all this into the Orbit Counting Theorem we have that the number of orbits m is, m = 1 24 (3 6 + 6 ⋅ 3 3 + 3 ⋅ 3 4 + 8 ⋅ 3 2 + 6 ⋅ 3 3) = 57. Hence the number of different cubes you can obtain by colouring the faces of a cube with three colours is 57.
